Q1/Q6 (organization/regeneration definitions) and Q4/Q5/Q7/Q8 (labile/stable/permanent cell classification) are each collapsed onto one concept -- the same underlying fact tested repeatedly.

questions.title: Organization means replacement by fibrous tissue
questions.question: Organization means replacement of the damaged tissue by:

options.B: New tissue of the same type

explanations.A: Incorrect. Calcified tissue is not a standard tissue-repair outcome -- dystrophic calcification can occur in dead tissue in some settings, but it does not define organization.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Replacement by new tissue of the same type describes regeneration, not organization -- these are the two distinct outcomes this lecture pairs against each other.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neural tissue is not a repair outcome at all; damaged neural tissue itself typically cannot regenerate (nerve cells are permanent cells) and instead undergoes organization like other permanent-cell tissue.
explanations.D: Correct. Organization means replacement of the damaged tissue by fibrous tissue. This scar fills the defect without restoring the original tissue type or function. It is the outcome that occurs when a tissue's own cells cannot regenerate it -- for example, permanent-cell tissue like nerve, cardiac or skeletal muscle.

questions.learning_objective: State that organization means replacement of damaged tissue by fibrous tissue.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Fibrous tissue"

questions.title: Post-appendectomy nodule with giant cells is granuloma formation
questions.question: A 25-year-old has an appendectomy, one month later she palpates a small nodule beneath the skin at the site of the healed sutured incision. The nodule is excised, and microscopic examination shows macrophages, collagen deposition, small lymphocytes, and multinucleated giant cells. A foreign refractile material is seen in the nodule. Which of the following complications of the surgery best accounts for these findings?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Exuberant granulation tissue is excess vascular and fibroblastic proliferation, without the giant cells and foreign material seen here.
explanations.B: Correct. Macrophages, collagen, lymphocytes and multinucleated giant cells surrounding a foreign refractile material describe a foreign-body granuloma. The retained suture material (the refractile particle) is the indigestible antigen provoking this macrophage-driven granulomatous reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyaline degeneration is extracellular protein deposition producing a glassy, homogeneous appearance, not a cellular reaction with giant cells and foreign material.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An abscess is a neutrophilic, pus-forming collection, not the macrophage-and-giant-cell picture with visible foreign material described here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a post-surgical nodule with macrophages, giant cells and foreign material as granuloma formation around retained suture.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Granuloma formation"

questions.title: A month-old myocardial infarction shows fibrous scar
questions.question: A 58-year-old man had chest pain persisting for 4 hours. A radiographic imaging procedure showed area of necrosis involving a 4-cm area of the posterior left ventricular free wall. Which of the following pathologic findings would most likely be seen in the left ventricular lesion 1 month later?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Liquefactive necrosis does not describe myocardial infarction healing -- it is characteristic of tissues like the brain, not the heart.
explanations.B: Correct. By one month after a myocardial infarction, the acute necrotic phase has already been replaced by mature fibrous scar tissue. Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells, so organization (fibrous scarring) is the only possible repair outcome for the necrotic myocardium. This is why a healed infarct is read as scar, not regenerated muscle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Coagulative necrosis is the acute-phase finding, present in the first days after infarction, not still present a month later once organization has completed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. True regeneration -- replacement by new cardiac muscle of the same type -- is not possible here, because cardiac myocytes are permanent cells that cannot regenerate.

questions.learning_objective: State that a myocardial infarction examined one month later shows fibrous scar, since cardiac myocytes are permanent cells.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Fibrous scar"

questions.title: Permanent cells never regenerate
questions.question: Cells which never regenerate are called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Labile cells regenerate continuously throughout adult life -- the opposite of never regenerating.
explanations.B: Correct. Permanent cells are cells which never regenerate once mature, with nerve cells (and cardiac and skeletal muscle) as the standard examples. Any significant damage to permanent-cell tissue can only heal by organization (fibrous scarring), never true regeneration.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Bone cells" names a specific tissue rather than a regenerative-capacity category, and bone itself is generally considered a stable-cell tissue capable of regeneration when stimulated, not a category that never regenerates.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Stable cells multiply when stimulated -- they retain regenerative capacity, just not the continuous, unstimulated kind labile cells have.

questions.learning_objective: Identify permanent cells as the class that never regenerates.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Permanent cells"

questions.title: Labile cells regenerate continuously during adult life
questions.question: Labile cells are:

options.A: Cells which regenerate continuously during adult life
options.B: Cells which multiply only when stimulated

explanations.A: Correct. Labile cells are cells which regenerate continuously during adult life, without needing a stimulus. Surface epithelium (mucous membranes, epidermis) and haematopoietic cells are the classic examples. They replace themselves on an ongoing basis, unlike stable cells, which need a stimulus first.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multiplying only when stimulated describes stable cells, which are normally quiescent, not labile cells, which regenerate continuously by default.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Muscle cells (cardiac and skeletal) are permanent cells, not labile cells -- they never regenerate once mature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cells which never multiply describes permanent cells, the opposite regenerative-capacity class from labile cells.

questions.title: Regeneration means replacement by the same tissue type
questions.question: Regeneration means:

options.A: Replacement of the damaged tissue by new one of the same type
options.B: Replacement of the damaged tissue by new one of the different type
options.C: Replacement of the damaged tissue by fibrosis
options.D: Replacement of the damaged tissue by granulation tissue

explanations.A: Correct. Regeneration means replacement of the damaged tissue by new tissue of the same type. It restores normal structure and function, unlike organization's fibrous scar. This outcome is possible only for labile and stable-cell tissue, not for permanent-cell tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Replacement by a different tissue type is not regeneration -- true regeneration specifically restores the original tissue type.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Replacement by fibrosis describes organization, the alternative outcome to regeneration, not regeneration itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Granulation tissue is the vascular, fibroblast-rich tissue that forms during organization/healing, an intermediate step toward a fibrous scar, not the definition of regeneration.

questions.learning_objective: State that regeneration means replacement of damaged tissue by new tissue of the same type.

questions.title: Stable cells multiply only when stimulated
questions.question: Stable cells are:

options.A: Cells which multiply only when stimulated
options.C: Cells which multiply continuously during life

explanations.A: Correct. Stable cells are cells which multiply only when stimulated. They are normally quiescent, held in the G0 phase, but capable of re-entering the cell cycle after injury. This is unlike labile cells, which regenerate continuously without needing a stimulus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cells which never multiply describes permanent cells, not stable cells, which retain regenerative capacity when stimulated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cells which multiply continuously during life describes labile cells, not stable cells, which are normally quiescent between stimuli.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Stabilizing the tissues" is not the defining property of stable cells -- their name refers to their regenerative-capacity category, not a structural stabilizing function.

questions.title: Nerve cells are an example of permanent cells
questions.question: Which of the following is an Examples of permanent cells?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mucous membranes are lined by labile epithelium, which regenerates continuously -- the opposite regenerative-capacity class from permanent cells.
explanations.B: Correct. Nerve cells are the standard example of permanent cells -- cells which never regenerate once mature, alongside cardiac and skeletal muscle. Damage to nerve tissue can only be repaired by organization (glial scarring in the CNS), never by regenerating new neurons.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Epidermis is a labile-cell tissue, continuously regenerating throughout adult life, not a permanent-cell example.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Haematopoietic cells are also a labile-cell tissue, with continuous turnover in the bone marrow, not an example of permanent cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify nerve cells as an example of permanent cells, distinct from labile tissues like mucous membranes, epidermis and haematopoietic cells.
